reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / ESC & ACC-AHA guidelines
clinicalPearls: Brugada syndrome is an inherited arrhythmia disorder characterised by a distinctive coved ST-segment elevation in the right precordial leads and a risk of polymorphic ventricular arrhythmia and sudden death in a structurally normal heart
Only the type 1 coved pattern is diagnostic; the saddleback type 2 pattern is suggestive and may need provocation or repositioned high leads to confirm
Arrhythmic events characteristically occur at rest or during sleep and may be triggered by fever, which can unmask the pattern
Certain drugs (including some sodium-channel blockers, and various psychotropic and anaesthetic agents) can precipitate or accentuate the pattern and should be avoided
It disproportionately affects young to middle-aged men and can present as syncope, nocturnal agonal breathing, or aborted sudden death
Diagnosis integrates the ECG pattern with clinical and family history, and a drug provocation test may be used when the resting ECG is non-diagnostic
An implantable cardioverter-defibrillator is the mainstay of protection in high-risk patients, and prompt treatment of fever is advised
Family screening and genetic counselling are important given autosomal dominant inheritance with variable expression
reference.pathophysiology: Brugada syndrome is most often linked to loss-of-function mutations in the cardiac sodium channel gene SCN5A, reducing inward sodium current. The leading explanation involves heterogeneity of repolarisation and depolarisation predominantly in the right ventricular outflow tract, producing a transmural voltage gradient that generates the characteristic ST-segment changes and a substrate for phase 2 reentry. This can trigger polymorphic ventricular tachycardia and ventricular fibrillation. Factors that reduce sodium current or increase transient outward current, such as fever and specific drugs, accentuate the abnormality and increase arrhythmic risk, which is why events cluster at rest, during sleep, and with febrile illness.
additionalDifferentials: Acute right precordial ST elevation from ischaemia or pericarditis
Electrolyte disturbance mimicking a Brugada pattern
Drug-induced or fever-induced phenocopies of the pattern
additionalInvestigations: 12-lead ECG including high right precordial lead placement to detect the coved pattern
Sodium-channel-blocker provocation testing under monitoring when the resting ECG is non-diagnostic
Assessment during febrile illness given fever-induced unmasking
Genetic testing and cascade family screening
Echocardiography or cardiac imaging to exclude structural disease such as ARVC
Electrophysiology study in selected cases for risk stratification
redFlags: MEDICAL EMERGENCY: polymorphic ventricular tachycardia or ventricular fibrillation causing syncope, cardiac arrest, or sudden death
Syncope or nocturnal agonal respiration in a patient with a type 1 pattern indicating high arrhythmic risk
Spontaneous (not drug-induced) type 1 pattern, which carries greater risk
Fever in a known patient, which can precipitate malignant arrhythmia
reference.prognosis: Asymptomatic individuals with only a drug-induced pattern generally have a low event rate, whereas those with a spontaneous type 1 pattern and prior syncope or aborted arrest are at substantially higher risk; defibrillator therapy and avoidance of triggers markedly improve outcomes in high-risk patients.
pitfalls: Treating a non-diagnostic saddleback pattern as definitive Brugada syndrome
Failing to place high right precordial leads or to consider provocation when suspicion is high
Prescribing drugs that can precipitate the pattern or omitting prompt fever control
Neglecting family screening after a diagnosis
management: Counsel on trigger avoidance, including prompt treatment of fever with antipyretics, avoidance of Brugada-aggravating drugs (certain sodium-channel blockers, psychotropic and anaesthetic agents) and moderation of alcohol
Implant a cardioverter-defibrillator in survivors of cardiac arrest or sustained ventricular arrhythmia and in high-risk symptomatic patients
Use quinidine, which reduces transient outward current, for recurrent arrhythmia, electrical storm or when a defibrillator is unsuitable or as adjunct to reduce shocks
Consider catheter ablation of the right ventricular outflow tract substrate for recurrent arrhythmia or frequent defibrillator shocks
Treat electrical storm acutely with isoprenaline infusion alongside aggressive fever control
Risk-stratify and monitor with attention to syncope, spontaneous type 1 pattern and, in selected cases, electrophysiology study
Offer genetic testing with cascade family screening and educate relatives on the drug-avoidance list and fever management
Refer to an inherited cardiac conditions and electrophysiology service for ongoing care
